cells.tense: You are here with the pen, seeing the pattern and holding the detail loosely.
cells.ask: Tell one person the pattern you've spotted in your own situation. Keep it plain, one detail they can check against what they know.
cells.core:
You can see the shape of a thing without needing every fact nailed down first. Someone describes a mess and you start hearing the machinery under it — what connects to what, what keeps repeating, where it's heading — and the picture holds itself together long enough for you to use it. That's rarer than it sounds. Most people only get there after the details have worn them down.

The half-light you work in is the point, not the obstacle. You don't need the whole road lit to take the next step, and you don't wait for it. What keeps this solid is carrying the pattern back to your own situation instead of leaving it up in the air. Nothing breaks if it doesn't hold. You still have the next honest step, and it usually shows itself.
cells.sheetLine: You see the pattern before the details get nailed down.
cells.verb: stripping what happened down to its pattern
cells.place: in half-light, taking the next step anyway

cells.tense: You are bracing at a future you keep trying to write in advance, pen pressing too hard.
cells.ask: Write the next step before you write the one after it. Give that single step a date you can point at, and leave the road past it blank.
cells.core:
The pattern-seeing hasn't stopped, it just went looking for something to protect you from. A conversation gets run forward, a decision gets a drawing of what it could turn into, and somewhere in there the next step stops being a step and becomes a rehearsal for everything that might follow.

Seeing mechanism finds a shape in anything you point it at. Feed it a future and it will draw the cables. You can't switch that off, and you don't have to. Put one piece of structure under today: a single next step with a date, clean and small, and let everything after it stay unlit on purpose. The plan doesn't need to cover the whole road for you to walk it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep building the whole road before you take a step.
cells.verb: stripping what happened down to its pattern
cells.place: in half-light, taking the next step anyway

cells.tense: You are standing at a door you already walked through, calling what you see names.
cells.ask: Take one thing you're already carrying and put it in front of someone. Let their story about it be part of what it means.
cells.core:
There's a way of reading what's happening — taking it at face value, calling a thing what it's called, moving on — that keeps everything manageable and keeps you out of the middle of it. Abstraction doesn't have to mean high theory. Refusing the second layer is abstraction too. You can get very good at the surface.

The second layer is where people actually meet, though. Nobody lives inside a fact. Sit with one story long enough and meaning shows up in it — yours, and the meaning someone else already found there. Someone close to you has a way of telling that story, a habit of handling a hard thing, and you can borrow it and still be yourself. That's what carrying something across looks like.
cells.sheetLine: Reading every layer and reading only the surface are both choices.

cells.tense: You have the pen down in a room you are already writing, and the room is keeping the receipts.
cells.ask: Say the rule you're running on, out loud, once. One sentence naming what you expect to happen next in some situation you're in.
cells.core:
There's a structure under the day that rarely gets said aloud. A way of predicting what a person will do, an expectation that keeps checking out, a line you know better than to cross with someone. It shows up like the tide, the way things go, the shape of how it is, and you move through it without stopping to look at it.

What's missing is a hand on the pen, some point in the day where the expectation gets named: this is what's coming next, and here is why. That one naming doesn't take anything away, doesn't make the place colder. It puts the writing back somewhere you can find it. One sentence, said to someone or said plainly to yourself.
cells.sheetLine: The rule you're following has been running without being said.
cells.verb: stripping what happened down to its pattern

attempts.check: The record gives mechanism, not history: Too Little says literalism and refusal of symbol, but nothing says what the person avoided or when, so no room, no person, no cost goes into that cell. A reader could reasonably say the pattern-seeing is not paranoia but plain accuracy about a life that is genuinely trap-laid, so the Too Much ask is a pause on building, not a denial that the pattern is there. The asks survive being wrong because each is one act with its own finish, useful whether or not the read lands. The sentence that serves me more than them is the Too Much 'the plan keeps the anxiety in business' — cut, since it grades the person's coping instead of describing the mechanism.
